question: Compare 'precision' as used in classification and as used for measurements.
answer: Precision in classification refers to the ratio of true positives to the sum of true positives and false positives, indicating how accurate the positive predictions are (S1). [S1] These definitions are distinct, with classification precision focusing on model accuracy in predicting positive outcomes, and measurement precision focusing on the consistency of individual measurements (S2) [S1] [S2].

citations.title: Ml Lecture Notes
citations.text: 4. Evaluation Metrics for Classification A confusion matrix counts true positives (TP), false positives (FP), true negatives (TN) and false negatives (FN). Accuracy is (TP + TN) divided by all examples. Accuracy is misleading on imbalanced data: a model that always predicts the majority class can reach 99% accuracy while detecting nothing. Precision = TP / (TP + FP) answers "of the examples predicted positive, how many are truly positive?". Recall (sensitivity) = TP / (TP + FN) answers "of the truly positive examples, how many did we find?". The F1 score is the harmonic mean of precision and recall: 2 * precision * recall / (precision + recall). Raising the decision threshold usually increases precision and lowers recall. The ROC curve plots the true positive rate against the false positive rate across thresholds, and AUC summarizes it: 0.5 is random guessing and 1.0 is perfect ranking.

citations.title: Statistics Confusable Terms
citations.text: standard deviation vs standard error: the standard deviation describes the spread of individual observations; the standard error describes the spread of a statistic such as the sample mean across repeated samples. confidence level vs confidence interval: the level (for example 95%) is a property of the procedure; the interval is the computed range of values. significance level vs p-value: alpha is chosen before the test; the p-value is computed from the data. covariance vs correlation: covariance carries the units of x times the units of y; correlation is unitless and always between -1 and 1. precision of a measurement: how close repeated measurements are to each other. Precision in classification is a different concept (see the machine learning course). normal: the normal distribution is the bell curve. It does not mean "typical" or "healthy" values.

S3.title: Ml Exercise Guide
S3.text:
Assignment 2: Choosing a Metric
Task. A fraud detection dataset has 1% fraudulent transactions. A teammate reports 99% accuracy. Decide whether the model is good.
Expected answer. Accuracy is not informative here because a model that predicts "not fraud" for everything also reaches 99%. Evaluate precision, recall, F1 and the precision-recall curve. In fraud detection, missing a fraud (a false negative) is usually costly, so recall is emphasized, while precision controls how many legitimate customers are inconvenienced.

S4.title: Ml Notation Abbreviations
S4.text: OOB: out-of-bag. In a random forest each tree is trained on a bootstrap sample, and the rows left out of that sample are the out-of-bag rows; about 36.8% (1/e) of the rows are out-of-bag for each tree. They provide a free validation estimate. MAE: mean absolute error. RMSE: root mean squared error. SGD: stochastic gradient descent. k-NN: k-nearest neighbors. PR AUC: area under the precision-recall curve; preferred over ROC AUC for strongly imbalanced classes. i.i.d.: independent and identically distributed. precision: in classification, TP / (TP + FP). It is not the same as measurement precision in statistics. sample: in machine learning a sample usually means one row of data (one example). In statistics a sample is a subset of a population. bias: the error from wrong assumptions of a model. The bias term (intercept) of a linear model is a different thing.
